title: Glimpsing the ox
hookLine: picture three: a glimpse, through sound and sight (Ox-Herding 3)
tomorrow: he's seen the ox. so why does it nearly drag him off?

cards: Tock. Zen remembers that small sound, and the monk who heard it, Xiangyan. Brilliant and full of answers, he was stumped by one question from his teacher, and he burned his notes.
The question was about his own face before his parents were born, and no book had the answer. He went off to tend a grave site and sweep. One day his broom flicked a pebble against a stalk of bamboo.
Tock. In that sound, the story says, he woke up.

teach.b: Kuoan's third picture is that moment. The preface says the herder finds the way through the sound he hears, and sees into the origin of things.
The verse: a bird sings on a branch, the sun is warm, the wind soft, willows green on the bank, and here the ox has nowhere left to hide.
Zen has a name for this glimpse: kensho, seeing your own nature. And here the tradition argues with itself.

teach.h: SUDDEN: ONE GLIMPSE IS THE OX.
teach.b: One side, the sudden school, carried by Huineng's line, says awakening is whole at once: one sound, and you see all of it. A glimpse of the ox is the ox. Their best case is Xiangyan himself: no ladder, one tock.
The other side, the gradual view, says the mind is cleared step by step, through daily training, and a glimpse fades unless you train.
A gradual reader could point to Kuoan's own series: after picture three come seven more, and in the very next one the ox nearly gets away. Yet Kuoan himself taught in Huineng's line.
Some later teachers held the two together: sudden seeing, slow living-it.
What neither side disputes is how the glimpse arrives: through plain senses, a bird, a pebble, bamboo.

how: Zen schools speak of kensho, seeing one's nature; some stress sudden awakening, others gradual training, and many teachers keep both. People on this path remember their own first glimpse and keep practicing after it.

games.q: your friend is sure awakening is sudden: one glimpse is the whole ox. state the gradual side's best case.
o: Kuoan's own series: after the glimpse come seven more pictures, and the ox nearly escapes.
glimpses are always imagination, so they shouldn't count for anything at all.
sudden awakening is a modern idea that no Zen teacher ever held.
games.why: the gradual view says a glimpse fades without training, and a gradual reader could point to Kuoan's series, which keeps going: picture four is the ox pulling hard. the sudden school answers with Xiangyan's one tock.

practice: Listen for one sound around you, the plainest one: a fan, a car, a bird outside. Let it be your bamboo for the two minutes, and if a memory of your own first glimpse on this path comes, let it sit beside the sound.

wordCard.voice: Glimpsing the ox: Kuoan's third picture. Through a sound and a sight, the herder sees what he's been looking for.

orig.note: Chinese: seeing one's nature; kensho in Japanese, Zen's word for the glimpse.

carryVoice: The line to keep: a glimpse, whole in a moment or the start of long work, and real either way. Three pictures in.
